{{Use American English|date = March 2019}}
{{Short description|Concept in abstract algebra}}
{{for|the minimal polynomial of a matrix|Minimal polynomial (linear algebra)}}

In [[field theory (mathematics)|field theory]], a branch of [[mathematics]], the '''minimal polynomial''' of an element <math>\alpha</math> of an [[Field extension|extension field]] of a [[Field (mathematics)|field]] is, roughly speaking, the [[polynomial]] of lowest [[degree of a polynomial|degree]] having coefficients in the smaller field, such that <math>\alpha</math> is a root of the polynomial. If the minimal polynomial of <math>\alpha</math> exists, it is unique. The coefficient of the highest-degree term in the polynomial is required to be 1.

More formally, a minimal polynomial is defined relative to a [[field extension]] <math>E/F</math> and an element of the extension field <math>E/F</math>. The minimal polynomial of an element, if it exists, is a member of <math>F[x]</math>, the [[Polynomial ring|ring of polynomials]] in the variable <math>x</math> with coefficients in <math>F</math>. Given an element <math>\alpha</math> of <math>E</math>, let <math>J_{\alpha}</math> be the set of all polynomials <math>f(x)</math> in <math>F[x]</math> such that <math>f(\alpha) = 0</math>. The element <math>\alpha</math> is called a [[Zero of a function|root or zero]] of each polynomial in <math>J_{\alpha}</math>.

More specifically, <math>J_{\alpha}</math> is the kernel of the [[ring homomorphism]] from <math>F[x]</math> to <math>E</math> which sends polynomials <math>g</math> to their value <math>g(\alpha)</math> at the element <math>\alpha</math>. Because it is the kernel of a ring homomorphism, <math>J_{\alpha}</math> is an [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] of the polynomial ring <math>F[x]</math>: it is closed under [[Polynomial#Operations|polynomial addition and subtraction]] (hence containing the zero polynomial), as well as under multiplication by elements of <math>F</math> (which is [[scalar multiplication]] if <math>F[x]</math> is regarded as a [[vector space]] over <math>F</math>).

The zero polynomial, all of whose coefficients are 0, is in every <math>J_{\alpha}</math> since <math>0\alpha^{i} = 0</math> for all <math>\alpha</math> and <math>i</math>. This makes the zero polynomial useless for classifying different values of <math>\alpha</math> into types, so it is excepted. If there are any non-zero polynomials in <math>J_{\alpha}</math>, i.e. if the latter is not the zero ideal, then <math>\alpha</math> is called an [[algebraic element]] over <math>F</math>, and there exists a [[monic polynomial]] of least degree in <math>J_{\alpha}</math>. This is the minimal polynomial of <math>\alpha</math> with respect to <math>E/F</math>. It is unique and [[irreducible polynomial|irreducible]] over <math>F</math>. If the zero polynomial is the only member of <math>J_{\alpha}</math>, then <math>\alpha</math> is called a [[transcendental element]] over <math>F</math> and has no minimal polynomial with respect to <math>E/F</math>.

Minimal polynomials are useful for constructing and analyzing field extensions. When <math>\alpha</math> is algebraic with minimal polynomial <math>f(x)</math>, the smallest field that contains both <math>F</math> and <math>\alpha</math> is [[Ring isomorphism|isomorphic]] to the [[quotient ring]] <math>F[x]/\langle f(x)\rangle</math>, where <math>\langle f(x)\rangle</math> is the ideal of <math>F[x]</math> generated by <math>f(x)</math>. Minimal polynomials are also used to define [[conjugate elements]].

== Definition ==

Let <math>E/F</math> be a [[field extension]], <math>\alpha</math> an element of <math>E</math>, and <math>F[x]</math> the ring of polynomials in <math>x</math> over <math>F</math>. The element <math>\alpha</math> has a minimal polynomial when <math>\alpha</math> is algebraic over <math>F</math>, that is, when <math>f(\alpha) = 0</math> for some non-zero polynomial <math>f(x)</math> in <math>F[x]</math>. Then the minimal polynomial of <math>\alpha</math> is defined as the monic polynomial of least degree among all polynomials in <math>F[x]</math> having <math>\alpha</math> as a root.

== Properties ==

Throughout this section, let <math>E/F</math> be a field extension over <math>F</math> as above, let <math>\alpha \in E</math> be an algebraic element over <math>F</math> and let <math>J_{\alpha}</math> be the ideal of polynomials vanishing on <math>\alpha</math>.

=== Uniqueness ===

The minimal polynomial <math>f</math> of <math>\alpha</math> is unique.

To prove this, suppose that <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are monic polynomials in <math>J_{\alpha}</math> of minimal degree <math>n > 0</math>. We have that <math>r := f - g \in J_{\alpha}</math> (because the latter is closed under addition/subtraction) and that <math>m := \deg(r) < n</math> (because the polynomials are monic of the same degree). If <math>r</math> is not zero, then <math>r / c_m</math> (writing <math>c_m \in F</math> for the non-zero coefficient of highest degree in <math>r</math>) is a monic polynomial of degree <math>m < n</math> such that <math>r / c_m \in J_{\alpha}</math> (because the latter is closed under multiplication/division by non-zero elements of <math>F</math>), which contradicts our original assumption of minimality for <math>n</math>. We conclude that <math>0 = r = f - g</math>, i.e. that <math>f = g</math>.

=== Irreducibility ===

The minimal polynomial <math>f</math> of <math>\alpha</math> is irreducible, i.e. it cannot be factorized as <math>f = gh</math> for two polynomials <math>g</math> and <math>h</math> of strictly lower degree.

To prove this, first observe that any factorization <math>f = gh</math> implies that either <math>g(\alpha) = 0</math> or <math>h(\alpha) = 0</math>, because <math>f(\alpha) = 0</math> and <math>F</math> is a field (hence also an [[integral domain]]). Choosing both <math>g</math> and <math>h</math> to be of degree strictly lower than <math>f</math> would then contradict the minimality requirement on <math>f</math>, so <math>f</math> must be irreducible.

=== Minimal polynomial generates <math>J_{\alpha}</math> ===

The minimal polynomial <math>f</math> of <math>\alpha</math> generates the ideal <math>J_{\alpha}</math>, i.e. every <math>g</math> in <math>J_{\alpha}</math> can be factorized as <math>g = fh</math> for some <math>h</math> in <math>F[x]</math>.

To prove this, it suffices to observe that <math>F[x]</math> is a [[principal ideal domain]], because <math>F</math> is a field: this means that every ideal <math>I</math> in <math>F[x]</math>, <math>J_{\alpha}</math> amongst them, is generated by a single element <math>f</math>. With the exception of the zero ideal <math>I = \{0\}</math>, the generator <math>f</math> must be non-zero and it must be the unique polynomial of minimal degree, up to a factor in <math>F</math> (because the degree of <math>fg</math> is strictly larger than that of <math>f</math> whenever <math>g</math> is of degree greater than zero). In particular, there is a unique monic generator <math>f</math>, and all generators must be irreducible. When <math>I</math> is chosen to be <math>J_{\alpha}</math>, for <math>\alpha</math> algebraic over <math>F</math>, then the monic generator <math>f</math> is the minimal polynomial of <math>\alpha</math>.

== Examples ==

=== Minimal polynomial of a Galois field extension ===
Given a [[Galois extension]] <math>L/K</math>, the minimal polynomial of any <math>\alpha \in L</math> not in <math>K</math> can be computed as
<math display="block">f(x) = \prod_{\sigma \in \text{Gal}(L/K)} (x - \sigma(\alpha))</math>
if <math>\alpha</math> has no stabilizers in the Galois action. Since it is irreducible, which can be deduced by looking at the roots of <math>f'</math>, it is the minimal polynomial. Note that the same kind of formula can be found by replacing <math>G = \text{Gal}(L/K)</math> with <math>G/N</math> where <math>N = \text{Stab}(\alpha)</math> is the stabilizer group of <math>\alpha</math>. For example, if <math>\alpha \in K</math> then its stabilizer is <math>G</math>, hence <math>(x - \alpha)</math> is its minimal polynomial.

=== Quadratic field extensions ===

==== Q(√2) ====
If <math>F = \mathbb{Q}</math>, <math>E = \mathbb{R}</math>, <math>\alpha = \sqrt{2}</math>, then the minimal polynomial for <math>\alpha</math> is <math>a(x) = x^2 - 2</math>. The base field <math>F</math> is important as it determines the possibilities for the coefficients of <math>a(x)</math>. For instance, if we take <math>F = \mathbb{R}</math>, then the minimal polynomial for <math>\alpha = \sqrt{2}</math> is <math>a(x) = x - \sqrt{2}</math>.

==== Q(√d) ====
In general, for the quadratic extension given by a square-free <math>d</math>, computing the minimal polynomial of an element <math>a + b\sqrt{d\,}</math> can be found using [[Galois theory]]. Then
<math display="block">\begin{align}
f(x) &= (x - (a + b\sqrt{d\,}))(x - (a - b\sqrt{d\,})) \\
&= x^2 - 2ax + (a^2 - b^2d)
\end{align}</math>
in particular, this implies <math>2a \in \mathbb{Z}</math> and <math>a^2 - b^2d \in \mathbb{Z}</math>. This can be used to determine <math>\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{d\,}\!\!\!\;\;)}</math> through a [[Quadratic integer#Determining the ring of integers|series of relations using modular arithmetic]].

=== Biquadratic field extensions ===
If <math>\alpha = \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3}</math>, then the minimal polynomial in <math>\mathbb{Q}[x]</math> is <math>a(x) = x^4 - 10x^2 + 1 = (x - \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{3})(x + \sqrt{2} - \sqrt{3})(x - \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3})(x + \sqrt{2} + \sqrt{3})</math>.

Notice if <math>\alpha = \sqrt{2}</math> then the Galois action on <math>\sqrt{3}</math> stabilizes <math>\alpha</math>. Hence the minimal polynomial can be found using the [[quotient group]] <math>\text{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{2},\sqrt{3})/\mathbb{Q})/\text{Gal}(\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt{3})/\mathbb{Q})</math>.

=== Roots of unity ===
The minimal polynomials in <math>\mathbb{Q}[x]</math> of [[root of unity|roots of unity]] are the [[cyclotomic polynomial]]s. The roots of the [[minimal polynomial of 2cos(2pi/n)|minimal polynomial of 2cos(2π/n)]] are twice the [[Complex number|real part]] of the primitive roots of unity.

=== Swinnerton-Dyer polynomials ===
The minimal polynomial in <math>\mathbb{Q}[x]</math> of the sum of the square roots of the first <math>n</math> [[Prime number|prime numbers]] is constructed analogously, and is called a [[Swinnerton-Dyer polynomial]].
